A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JALMBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, support comparison. Revised settings and relocated material can be identified.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak evaluations, voice and representation analyses, defense experiments, white-box attack results, and OpenBookQA utility measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports revised benchmark results and original ICA prefix-length, TTS-system and human-voice experiments, including results in its appendices.

M1.justification: The modular benchmark framework and underlying attack and defense methods remain unchanged. ICA's new prefix-length sweep changes evaluation settings for an existing attack; it does not introduce a proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Section 3 expands the AdvBench-derived harmful-query corpus to curated instructions from AdvBench, JailbreakBench, MM-SafetyBench and HarmBench. Evaluation also adds three TTS engines and recordings from six human speakers, substantially extending audio-source coverage. The nine non-English languages and OpenBookQA task were already covered.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 12 ALMs, eight attack methods, five defenses and three white-box target models. Added TTS engines vary input generation. Figure 1's new benchmark comparison describes capabilities rather than introducing experimentally evaluated attack or defense competitors.

E3.justification: The base evaluation grows from 50 to 246 harmful instructions. ICA changes from a fixed three-example prefix to testing one, two and three examples, reporting success across settings as ASR@3. Topic analysis replaces GPT-generated categories and manual confirmation with policy-based categories and independent annotation plus adjudication. New voice experiments introduce a six-speaker evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ICA context-length sensitivity analysis in Appendix C.1/Table 7 and tests dependence on synthesis engine and human speech in Table 3/Appendix C.4. Topic analysis is substantially revised. White-box AdvWave, representation visualization and defense–utility analyses already existed and are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 newly reports two independent topic annotators, third-annotator adjudication and Cohen's kappa of 0.93. Neither version reports seeded repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals for ASR; the existing score-distribution boxplots are retained.

E6.justification: Many attack, defense, voice, topic and white-box results are replaced, and new experimental entries appear. Audio ICA averages change from 10.8% to 42.3%, with changed corpus and ASR@3 settings; black-box AdvWave averages change from 97.3% to 96.2% on the expanded corpus. These are not same-setting performance changes. OpenBookQA accuracies remain unchanged. v2 also introduces conflicting result assignments: Table 4 labels 42.3% as DAN, whereas Table 1 assigns it to ICA.

T1.justification: The four AMSE transformation equations are retained, moving from v1 Appendix C.3.3 to v2 Appendix B.4.3. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added or revised. ASR@3 introduces an evaluation aggregation rule, not new theoretical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction drop the unqualified first-comprehensive-benchmark wording. Section 2 narrows novelty to jointly evaluating diverse existing LLM/ALM attacks and transferable defenses. The central benchmark, vulnerability and defense–utility contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 changes the interpretation of accent variation from exposing notable vulnerabilities to generally having minimal impact, although v2's introduction retains the earlier emphasis. Architectural safety transfer moves from a tentative hypothesis to a claimed decisive mechanism, with an added joint-alignment explanation. Limitations are revised after adding TTS and human recordings, emphasizing remaining speaker and prosody coverage gaps.

D1.justification: v2 documents generation settings for additional TTS engines and human recordings, and updates total computation from approximately 2,380 to 6,000 GPU-hours. It replaces direct GitHub/Hugging Face access links with an anonymous code/data link. In-PDF query-label and SSJ masked-word lists are removed, with readers instead directed to the repository or dataset.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the assertion that earlier audio evaluations did not focus on jailbreaks with explicit positioning against JABench and the newly cited Audio Jailbreak benchmark. Figure 1 adds a feature comparison with these competitors. References also add dataset and TTS works while pruning broader LLM-safety citations, substantially revising the benchmark's research positioning.

P1.justification: The introduction is reorganized into dataset, evaluation, analysis and defense summaries. Architecture analysis, mitigation discussion and the conclusion are substantially rewritten. Appendices reorganize model details, experimental settings and analyses; social impacts move from the main text to Appendix E, and lengthy query listings disappear.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is extensively redesigned around the workflow and benchmark comparison. Table 3 gains TTS/human columns while language results move to Appendix Table 10 and receive a new summary plot. An ICA sensitivity table is added, several tables lose summary columns or rows, and representation and mitigation displays are redrawn or relocated.

improvement.justification: The broader corpus, ICA sensitivity test and TTS/human-speech experiments address important coverage and evaluation limitations in v1. However, v2 introduces central reporting conflicts: Table 4 misassigns attack names relative to Tables 1–2, and GLM-4-Voice's harmful-audio baseline is 19.5% in Table 1 but 26.4% in Table 3. These inconsistencies undermine interpretation of the revised comparisons. The benefits and reliability problems prevent a confident net quality judgment from the PDFs.
